### Packages and Data

```{r load-packages, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE}
library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)

```

## Data set: college recent grads

```{r, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(fivethirtyeight)
college_grad_df <- college_recent_grads
# First look at your data set
glimpse(college_grad_df)
```


# Exercise 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

```{r}

college_grad_df %>% ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x= median), fill = "plum")

college_grad_df %>% ggplot() +
  geom_histogram(aes(x= median), fill = "palevioletred", binwidth = 2500)


college_grad_df %>%
  count(major_category, sort = TRUE)

```

_With a bandwidth of 2500, the histogram provides greater detail as the specified bandwidth is smaller than the standard, resulting in more bars. Regardless, the model is right leaning, leading to a positive skew, the count peaking/concentrated around a median of 3.5e+04. It also seems like there is a potential outlier around 1.1e+05_


# Exercise 2: Exploring relationship

```{r}
college_grad_df %>% drop_na(sharewomen, median) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = sharewomen, y= median)) +
  geom_point(colour = "plum") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "palevioletred") 


coef(lm(median ~ sharewomen, data = college_grad_df))

```

_From the scatter plot, there is a distinct negative correlation between a higher share of women and majors with lower median earnings, the formula of the line of best fit being: y = 56100 - 30700x, where y is median and x is sharewomen. Additionally, the negative gradient of -30700 indicates that for every 1 unit increase in the proportion of women, the predicted median earnings decrease by roughly $30,700._

# Exercise 3: Fit and interpret a numerical predictor

```{r}

share_fit = linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(median ~ sharewomen, data = college_grad_df)

tidy(share_fit)

glance(share_fit)

share_fit_aug = augment(share_fit$fit)

share_fit_aug %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray", lty = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")



```

_median = 56100 - 30700 sharewomen, is the formula of the fitted model. The negative gradient of -30700 indicates that for every 1 unit increase in the proportion of women, the predicted median earnings decrease by roughly $30,700 - just like the initial visualisation._

_Doesn't seem like there is a distinct trend or pattern, insinuating that a linear model may be suitable to model the data, however one could argue that the scatter plots fan out slightly at the end as the fitted values increase._

# Exercise 4: Consider a categorical variable instead 

```{r}

college_grad_df = college_grad_df %>% mutate(
  engineering = case_when(
    str_detect(major, regex("engineering", ignore_case = TRUE)) ~ "Engineering",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  )
)

share_fit2 = linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(median ~ engineering, data = college_grad_df)

tidy(share_fit2)

glance(share_fit2)

share_fit2_aug = augment(share_fit2$fit)

share_fit2_aug %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray", lty = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")

levels(as.factor(college_grad_df$engineering))


```

_The baseline category is Engineering. The intercept of 58,388.46 represents the average median earnings of Engineering majors, approximately $58,388.46. The slope of -21,462.61 indicates that Other majors have average median earnings approximately $21,462.61 lower than Engineering majors, giving them predicted average median earnings of $36,925.85._

## Data set: Beauty in the classroom

```{r read-data}
evals<-read.csv("data/evals.csv", row.names=1)
```


# Exercise 1: Exploratory Data Analysis

1.  Visualize the distribution of `score` in the dataframe `evals`.

```{r viz-score}

evals %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = score)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.25, fill = "plum") 

evals %>%
  summarise(
    mean = mean(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(score, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(score, na.rm = TRUE)
  )



```

_Model is left leaning, hence resulting in a negative skew showing that students generally rate courses higher._

2.  Visualize and describe the relationship between `score` and `bty_avg` using `geom_point()` to represent the data. 

```{r scatterplot}

evals %>% drop_na(score, bty_avg) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bty_avg, y= score)) +
  geom_point(colour = "plum", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "palevioletred") 

evals %>% drop_na(score, bty_avg) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bty_avg, y= score)) +
  geom_jitter(colour = "mediumpurple") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "cornflowerblue") 

```

_Jitter adds small amount of noise. Multiple observations share identical bty_avg and score values. These observations overlap, making them appear as a single point. This creates the misleading impression that there are fewer observations in certain regions than there actually are. Jitter makes the density and frequency of observations easier to see._

# Exercise 2: Simple Linear regression with a numerical predictor

1. Fit a linear model called `score_bty_fit` to predict average professor evaluation `score` from average beauty rating (`bty_avg`). Print the regression output using `tidy()`.

```{r fit-score_bty_fit}
# remove eval = FALSE from the code chunk options after filling in the blanks
score_bty_fit <- linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(score ~ bty_avg, data = evals)
```

```{r tidy-score_bty_fi}
# remove eval = FALSE from the code chunk options after filling in the blanks
tidy(score_bty_fit)
```

_score = 3.880 + 0.067bty_avg._

2. Plot the data again using `geom_jitter()`, and add the regression line.

```{r viz-score_bty_fit}

evals %>% drop_na(score, bty_avg) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bty_avg, y= score)) +
  geom_jitter(colour = "mediumpurple") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "cornflowerblue") 


```

3. Interpret the slope of the linear model in context of the data.

_The gradient of the regression line tells you how much the predicted score changes for every 1-unit increase in bty_avg._

4. Interpret the intercept of the linear model in context of the data. Comment on whether or not the intercept makes sense in this context.

_The model shows that as bty_avg increases, so does score. The intercept represents the predicted teaching score for a lecturer with an average beauty rating of 0._

5. Determine the $R^2$ of the model and interpret it in the context of the data.

```{r R2}
# remove eval = FALSE from the code chunk options after filling in the blanks
glance(score_bty_fit)
```

_the r squared value is 0.03502226, representing the proportion of variation in score that is explained by the linear regression model using bty_avg._

6. Make a plot of residuals vs. predicted values for the model above.

```{r viz-score_bty_fit-diagnostic}
# remove eval = FALSE from the code chunk options after filling in the blanks
score_bty_aug <- augment(score_bty_fit$fit)


score_bty_aug %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = .fitted, y = .resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "gray", lty = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Fitted values", y = "Residuals")

```

# Exercise 4: Multiple linear regression

1. Fit a multiple linear regression model, predicting average professor evaluation `score` based on average beauty rating (`bty_avg`) and `gender.`

```{r fit-score_bty_gender_fit}
score_bty_gender_fit = linear_reg() %>%
  set_engine("lm") %>%
  fit(score ~ bty_avg + gender, data = evals)

tidy(score_bty_gender_fit)

glance(score_bty_gender_fit)

levels(as.factor(evals$gender))

```

*Add your narrative here.*

```{r}
evals %>%
  drop_na(score, bty_avg, gender) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = bty_avg, y = score, colour = gender)) +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE)

coef(lm(score ~ bty_avg, data = evals))

temp = evals %>% filter(gender == "female")

coef(lm(score ~ bty_avg, data = temp))

temp = evals %>% filter(gender == "male")

coef(lm(score ~ bty_avg, data = temp))

```

2. What percent of the variability in `score` is explained by the model `score_bty_gender_fit`. 

```{r}
glance(score_bty_gender_fit)
```
_5.9% of the variation in score is explained by the model - as shown by the r squared value._

3. What is the equation of the line corresponding to just male professors?

_score = 3.74733824	+ 0.17238955gendermen_

4. For two professors who received the same beauty rating, which gender tends to have the higher course evaluation score?

_Depends on the score, higher the score, male teachers tend to have the higher course evaluation score, however for low scores, female teachers tend to have the higher course evaluation score._

5. How does the relationship between beauty and evaluation score vary between male and female professors?

_Males have a steeper slope/gradient than the lobf for females, etc..._

6. How do the adjusted $R^2$ values of `score_bty_fit` and `score_bty_gender_fit` compare? 

```{r }
# remove eval = FALSE from the code chunk options after filling in the blanks
glance(score_bty_fit)$adj.r.squared
glance(score_bty_gender_fit)$adj.r.squared
```

_As the r squared value of score_bty_fit is 3.29% and score_bty_gender_fit is 5.50%, the model considering gender as well has a substantially larger percentage showing that the model can explain more of the variation of the the socre variable, hence showing that it is a more suitable/better model over the first model of score_bty_fit._

7. Compare the slopes of `bty_avg` under the two models (`score_bty_fit` and `score_bty_gender_fit`).

_The gradient for score_bty_fit of 0.06663704, and for score_bty_gender_fit, the gradient is 0.07415537, showing that when considering gender as well, the gradient is steeper..._
